messages.content: I push open the door of the inn, shake the rain from my coat, and look for whoever is in charge. "A room for the night, if you have one. And something hot."

The Heron's Rest is a low-beamed room that smells of peat smoke and boiled barley. Three tables are taken by marsh men who glance up at the draught and go back to their dice. Behind the bar, a broad woman in her fifties with grey hair pinned under a kerchief is wiping a tankard with the corner of her apron. She studies your soaked coat, the leather satchel, the brass tube of the map case across your back.

"There's one room left, over the kitchen, so it's warm at least," she says. "Four pence with supper. Stew tonight, eel and leek." She sets the tankard down and holds out a hand, palm up, in the manner of someone who has been cheated before. "Pay now and I'll have the girl carry up water. You've come up the south road in this? There's been nobody through since noon."

One of the dice players, a thin man with a red scarf, has stopped playing to listen.
I count four pence onto the bar and lower my voice. "I'd rather not say much with an audience. Is there somewhere quieter I can eat?"

The woman follows your glance to the man in the red scarf and gives a short nod, as if this confirms something she already suspected about him. "Kitchen," she says, and lifts the hinged end of the bar to let you through.

The kitchen is hot and crowded with hanging pots. A girl of about twelve is scrubbing turnips at a basin; the woman sends her off to air the room upstairs. She ladles stew into a bowl, cuts bread, and puts both on the scarred table by the hearth.

"I'm Hesper Quill. This house has been mine for nineteen years and nothing said at this table has ever walked out of the door." She pulls out the stool opposite and sits, folding her arms. "That one out there is Dunmore's man. He sits in my taproom and counts strangers for whoever pays him. So. Who are you, and should I be worried about you sleeping under my roof?"

"My name is Mara Venn. I'm a cartographer, hired by the Pilots' Guild in Greywater to chart the estuary. A rival would pay well to know where I am, so I don't give my name on the road. You're the first person I've told since I left the south, and I'd like it to stay that way."

Hesper considers this for the time it takes the fire to settle. Then she unfolds her arms.

"Mara Venn," she repeats quietly, as though fitting the name to your face. "Well, Mara, it stays in this kitchen. Out there you're a traveller who paid in advance, and that's all anyone in my taproom needs." She pushes the bread closer to you. "The Guild's been asking for a proper chart since the Wren went down on the bar two winters back. Eleven men. If you're the one they finally sent, you'll find friends in Greywater. You'll also find the people who liked the estuary better when nobody could read it."

She gets up to stir a pot, and speaks with her back to you. "It's four days north on foot along the harbor road, five if the Wick is in flood. I can tell you where to sleep and who to avoid. Ask what you like."
I reach across the hearth for the bread knife and my sleeve catches the handle of the oil lamp on the shelf. I try to steady it.

The lamp tips before your hand closes on it. Hot oil runs down the shelf and over your left forearm, and it burns at once. The lamp itself rolls, and Hesper catches it against her hip without looking, the way a woman catches a falling child.

"Cold water, now. Don't rub it." She has your wrist in a firm grip and is steering your arm into the turnip basin before the sentence is finished. The water is shockingly cold. A red band is already rising across the inside of your left forearm, a hand's width below the elbow, about as long as your palm.

"It'll blister, but it's clean," Hesper says after a long look. She takes a pot of green salve from a shelf, comfrey by the smell, and a roll of linen. "Keep it there while I count to two hundred. Then I'll dress it. You'll want to change that bandage every evening and keep the arm out of salt water, which on this coast is easier said than done." She starts counting under her breath.

While she bandages my arm, I take the brass compass out of my satchel with my good hand and set it on the table to check it wasn't damaged when I knocked the shelf. "My brother Edrin gave me this before he sailed. The glass was already cracked."

Hesper ties off the linen with a flat knot and turns the compass toward the firelight with one finger, careful not to lift it. It is a pocket instrument of old brass, worn smooth at the hinge. A single crack runs across the glass from the north point to the rim, fine as a hair. Under it the needle swings, hesitates, and settles.

"Still true," she says. "My husband had one like it. Not as good." She reads the engraving inside the lid, lips moving: a small heron, and the initials E.V. "Edrin Venn. He's at sea, then?" She does not wait for an answer you might not want to give. "Keep it inside your coat on the road. Brass like that is worth a month's wages in Thornby, and a cracked glass doesn't lower the price as much as you'd think."

From the taproom comes the scrape of a bench. Hesper tilts her head, listening. "That'll be Dunmore's man leaving to make his report. A woman with a map case, travelling alone, no name given. That's all he has." She looks rather pleased about it.
In the morning I come down early with my pack. "Thank you for last night, Hesper. What do I need to know about the road north?"

The kitchen is grey with dawn and smells of fresh bread. Hesper is already kneading, floured to the elbows. She points her chin at a cloth bundle on the table: a loaf, a wedge of hard cheese, a twist of salt.

"For the road. Don't argue, Mara, you paid for supper and ate half of it." She keeps working the dough while she talks. "First day is the causeway across Sallow Fen. Stay on the stones; the green on either side will hold a heron and nothing heavier. There's an eel-catcher out there named Tobin, deaf in one ear, honest. Second night, there's a salt-boiler's hut past the dunes. Third day you cross the Wick at the ford, and if the bridge is down again you wait, you do not wade. After that it's Thornby market, then the cliff path to Greywater."

She wipes her hands and, for the first time, comes around the table. She checks the knot on your bandage, nods, and opens the back door onto the yard so that you need not pass through the taproom. Mist lies over the fen. "Go quietly. And if you come back this way, the room over the kitchen is yours."
I follow the causeway out across the fen, keeping to the stones as I was told, and watch for the eel-catcher.

The causeway is a single line of flat grey stones, each a long stride from the next, laid across water the colour of strong tea. Reeds stand higher than your head on both sides. Where the mist thins you can see how far the fen runs: to the edge of the sky in every direction, with the inn already a dark smudge behind you.

Toward mid-morning you hear wood knocking on wood. A punt is nosed into the reeds a few yards off the stones, and a wiry man in a sealskin cap is lifting wicker traps out of the water and shaking them into a tub. He does not turn at your footsteps. Only when your shadow falls across his tub does he look up, and he cups a hand behind his right ear at once.

"You'll have to talk to this side," he says, too loudly. "The other's been shut since a mast came down on it." His eyes go to the cloth bundle tied to your pack and he grins, showing four teeth. "That's Hesper's bread. She only ties that knot for people she's taken to. Tobin Marsh. What does a friend of Hesper's want on my fen?"
I keep the map case behind my shoulder and speak toward his good ear. "She said you were honest. I'm going north to Greywater. Is the causeway sound all the way across?"

"Honest," Tobin repeats, pleased, as if it were a rare fish. "It's sound as far as the Widow's Elbow. After that there's three stones gone under since the rains, and the gap's wider than you can jump with a pack on. People try it. I find their hats."

He drops the last trap into the punt and wipes his hands down his jerkin. "I'll pole you round the gap. No charge to one of Hesper's, but you can hold the tub steady while I work the far line, since I've only the two hands."

His gaze has drifted past your shoulder while he talks. However you stand, the brass end of the case shows above your pack, and he nods at it. "That's a chart tube. My cousin sailed with a man who had one. So you're a mapmaker." He seems entirely satisfied with this, and does not ask for anything more. "Well, mapmaker? In you get, or stay and jump. The eels don't mind which."
I climb into the punt and steady the tub between my knees. "Has anyone else come along the causeway this morning?"

The punt rocks, settles, and slides out of the reeds as Tobin leans on his pole. The tub is half full of eels, brown and green, tying and untying themselves; cold water slops over your boots.

"One," Tobin says. "Before sunrise, which is no hour for an honest man to be on the stones. Thin fellow, red scarf, walking fast with no pack. He stood where you stood and asked had a woman gone by with a brass case, and what was she called." He spits neatly over the side. "I told him I was deaf. That's half true, and half was all he'd paid for."

He poles in silence past a place where the causeway simply stops. Three stones lie under a hand's depth of water, furred with weed, and beyond them the line picks up again. "He went on north. Toward the salt pans, I'd say, there's nothing else that way before the river." Tobin glances at you sideways, with the first sign of real curiosity. "He didn't know what you were called. I noticed that. Seemed to me it bothered him a good deal."
At the far side of the gap I step back onto the stones and hold out a penny. "For the crossing. And if he comes back this way, you never saw me."

Tobin looks at the penny as though it might bite him and closes your fingers over it with his own wet hand.

"Saw who? A mapmaker with no name is nobody at all, and I can't tell a man what I never heard." He rummages under the thwart and comes up with something long wrapped in dock leaves, which he pushes into your arms before you can refuse it. It is warm and smells of oak smoke. "Smoked this morning. Eat it tonight, it won't keep past tomorrow."

He points north with the pole. The stones run on toward a low pale line that must be the dunes. "Two hours to dry ground. After that, follow the posts with the white paint on them, and only those. There's a low stretch the tide takes at dusk, so don't dawdle looking at birds. The salt-boiler's a widow called Ilsa. She'll seem hard. She isn't."

He is already backing the punt into the reeds, one hand lifted, his deaf side turned toward anything else you might say.
I follow the white posts through the dunes toward the smoke, and call out well before I reach the hut. "Hello the house! A traveller, looking for a dry floor tonight."

The salt pans lie behind the last dune like a row of grey mirrors: shallow clay basins, a dozen of them, each rimmed with a white crust. At the far end stands a turf-roofed hut with a lean-to boiling shed, and the smoke you have been following rises from an iron pan as wide as a cart, set over a trench of glowing driftwood.

A woman straightens from the pan with a long wooden rake in her hands. She is perhaps forty, raw-boned, her forearms white to the elbow with dried brine. A boy's face appears round the door of the hut behind her and is not withdrawn.

"I heard you. They heard you in Thornby." She looks you over without hurry: boots, pack, the bandage showing at your cuff, the brass case. "Ilsa Brandt. A dry floor's a penny. Supper you'll rake for, miss, because I'm a hand short since my man drowned and the pan won't wait for anyone's manners." She holds the rake out toward you, handle first, and waits to see what you do with it.
I pay the penny and take the rake in my right hand, keeping the bandaged arm against my chest. "Show me how it's done."

Ilsa pockets the penny and shows you once, briskly. The rake goes in at the far edge of the pan, flat, and is drawn toward you so that the crust comes away in a wet grey sheet and heaps against the rim. Then the heap is lifted into a wicker cone to drain. The heat off the pan dries your face tight in a moment, and the steam tastes of the sea.

"Slower. You're not mowing hay. Let it come to you." She watches three more strokes, grunts, and leaves you to it while she feeds the trench.

The boy has crept out and sat down on an upturned basket where he can see you work. He is about nine, with his mother's long jaw and a scab on each knee. For a while he says nothing. Then, in the clear carrying voice of a child who has been told not to ask things, he says, "What happened to your arm?"

"Pim." Ilsa does not turn round. "Leave the lady's arm where it is."

Pim goes on looking at the bandage anyway, and then at you, plainly still hoping for an answer.
"A burn, from lamp oil. It's healing." I draw the rake in again and nod toward the north. "Did a man in a red scarf come by here today?"

Pim nods hard, glad to have been asked something, but it is his mother who answers. She has stopped feeding the fire.

"Noon. He bought nothing and he sat on my wall as if he'd paid for it." Ilsa knocks a brand deeper into the trench with her heel. "He wanted to know about a woman with a brass case. Which way she'd gone, what she was called. He offered the boy a halfpenny."

"I said nobody came," Pim says, "because nobody had, then." He considers. "I'd have liked the halfpenny."

"He's Dunmore's," Ilsa goes on. "Dunmore holds the lease on half these pans and I pay him rent on quarter day. That's all I owe him. I don't owe him my eyes." She looks at the case on your back, and then away from it, deliberately. "He said he'd wait at the Wick ford, where the bridge is, since everyone going north must cross there. That's what he believes. There's an old carters' track from the back of the dunes to a rope ferry two miles upstream. It's rough going, miss, and it's where I'd walk, if I were whoever he's after."
After supper I unwrap my arm by the fire to change the dressing, and ask Ilsa if she can spare a strip of clean linen. Then I hold the compass out to Pim. "Do you want to see how this works?"

Ilsa tears a long strip from a washed flour sack and brings the rushlight close before she gives it to you. She studies the burn with the frankness of someone who has seen a good many. "Blistered and ugly, and no red creeping from it. Whoever dressed that first knew what they were about." She hands over the strip and a cup of water that has been boiled, and goes back to scouring the pot.

Pim takes the compass in both hands as if it were an egg. He turns the brass case over, runs a thumbnail along the crack in the glass, and frowns at it. "It's broken."

It is not, as he finds when he turns in a circle on the earth floor and the needle refuses to turn with him. He does it again, faster, and then sits down hard. He opens the lid and traces the marks cut inside it with one finger, slowly, though it is clear from his face that he cannot read them.

"It always knows," he says, with deep respect. He looks up at you across the fire. "Who gave it to you?"
At dawn I thank Ilsa and take the carters' track she described, staying well away from the main road.

The track is two ruts through gorse and standing water, and it takes most of the morning. You hear the Wick before you see it: a low steady roar, like wind in a chimney. Then the gorse opens and the river is in front of you, brown and fast and far wider than it has any right to be, carrying whole bushes along on its back.

The ferry is a flat-bottomed boat the size of a barn door, tied to a rope as thick as your wrist that runs from a post on this bank to a post on the other. Nobody is tending it. On the slope above the landing a cart loaded with sacks has sunk one wheel to the axle in mud. A grey mule stands in the shafts with his ears back, and a very large man in a leather apron is addressing him by name.

"Bishop, you were born in a ditch and I'll see you buried in one." He catches sight of you and does not lower his voice at all. "Stranger! If you've two hands and a back, lend them here. Odo Fenn will owe you a favour, and Bishop will owe you an apology he hasn't the grace to make."
I set down my pack and put my shoulder to the wheel beside him. "On three. And I need to get across as well. Does the ferry take passengers?"

Odo counts, the mule decides at the last instant to cooperate, and the wheel comes out of the mud with a sound like a boot leaving a bog. The cart lurches onto the firm ground by the landing. Odo straightens up, a full head taller than you, and wipes his palms on his apron with great satisfaction.

"It takes whoever I say. It's my cousin's ferry, and my cousin's in Thornby selling a horse he doesn't own, so today I'm ferryman and toll-keeper both." He jerks his chin at the river. "She's high. I'd not take her alone with the cart, the boat swings too much with nobody on the pole. So there's your fare paid, if you'll stand at the upstream side and keep us off whatever comes down."

He begins checking the mule's harness, and while he does it his eye travels along the brass case on your pack with open, good-natured nosiness.

"Now what's in that? Too long for a flute. Fishing rod? My wife's brother carries his fiddle bow in a thing like that, but he hasn't your boots." He waits, grinning, in no doubt at all that he will be told.
"Charts. I draw maps for a living." I take the mule's bridle on the other side and help lead him down to the boat. "I'm told a man is watching the lower ford. Thin, with a red scarf."

"A mapmaker! Then you can tell me where I am, for Bishop surely can't." Odo laughs at his own joke, then snorts. "I saw your man from the ridge at first light. Sat on the bridge wall like a crow on a gibbet. He'll not see us. The ford's a mile down and there's alder all the way between."

Bishop stops dead at the plank. Odo takes off his hat, claps it over the mule's eyes, and walks him aboard blind. The cart follows with a hollow rumble, and the boat sinks until the river is a hand's breadth below the side. Odo casts off and begins to haul on the rope, hand over hand.

The current takes hold at once. The boat swings out on its tether and leans; water piles up brown against the upstream side, and the rope creaks from one end to the other. You are perhaps halfway when Odo looks up the river and stops laughing.

An entire tree is coming down on the flood, roots first, turning slowly, straight for the boat.

"Mapmaker! The pole, by your foot! Get it on that trunk and shove, or it'll take the rope and us with it!"
I snatch up the pole, brace it against the trunk as it comes, and push with everything I have until it slides past the stern.

The pole strikes bark and bends. The whole weight of the tree comes up through the wood into your shoulders, and for the space of two breaths the boat, the trunk and the river all seem to be deciding the matter between them. Then the roots swing wide. The trunk grinds down the length of the boat with a noise like a cart on gravel, clears the stern by the width of a hand, and goes on toward the sea.

The rope holds. Odo hauls the last thirty yards without a word and runs the boat up onto shingle. Only then does he let out a breath and begin to laugh again, louder than before.

"Well shoved! I've had men aboard who'd have prayed instead." He uncovers Bishop's eyes; the mule looks about him with contempt. "I turn off for my farm at the heath shrine, an hour on. Ride on the tail of the cart that far and rest your arms."

He has noticed the linen at your cuff, dark and dripping where the river came over the side. "That's wet through. River water, mind, not salt. The Sister at the shrine keeps bees and dressings both. She'll see to it and ask nothing for it."
I ride on the back of the cart as far as the shrine, climb down, wave to Odo, and knock at the door. "Sister? A traveller with a burn that wants looking at."

The shrine is a squat building of grey fieldstone with a turf roof, standing alone where four heath tracks meet. A row of straw bee skeps is lined along its south wall, and even this late in the year a few bees are crawling on the warm stone. Odo's cart rattles away down the western track, his arm still raised.

The door is opened by a tall woman of about sixty in an undyed habit, the sleeves rolled above the elbow and a bee veil pushed up onto her forehead. Her hands are sticky to the wrist. She looks at your face first, then at your cuff, and seems to reach a conclusion about both.

"Travellers with burns I can manage before supper. Travellers with sins take longer, and I charge them in firewood." She steps back from the door. "I'm Sister Avel. Come in and sit by the window where the light is. Mind the frames on the floor, I'm in the middle of taking the last of the comb."

Inside it smells of wax and smoke. There is one bench, one table, and a shelf crowded with stoppered jars. She rinses her hands in a basin and turns to you, waiting to be shown.
I unwrap the wet linen and hold out my arm. "It was dressed with comfrey the first night. It got soaked this morning, crossing the Wick."

Sister Avel takes your wrist and turns the arm to the window. Her fingers are cool and entirely steady. The blister has broken under the wet linen and the skin beneath is pink and raw, but she presses along its edges and nods.

"No heat in it and no smell. Comfrey was the right beginning; whoever chose it had sense." She reaches down a jar without looking for it. "Now it's open, we change the treatment. Honey, to keep the rot out. Nothing spoils in honey. And a little yarrow to bring the skin together." She spreads the mixture thinly, lays a pad of clean lint over it and binds the arm with quick overlapping turns. It stings, and then it eases.

"I don't ask names at this door," she says, tying off. "Half of those who knock would be obliged to lie to me, and I'd sooner not be the occasion of it. But I do ask where a person is bound, because the heath has four roads and three of them are mistakes." She sits back on her heels and looks at you with frank grey eyes. "Where are you going, child?"
"Greywater. But there's a man following me, and I'd be glad if he came to believe otherwise."

Sister Avel receives this as calmly as she received the burn. She gets up, wipes her fingers, and begins fitting a honeycomb frame back into its box while she thinks.

"A pedlar came through at noon and said there was a fellow at the Wick bridge stopping every woman on the road. A thin man. He'll have worked out by now that he was sitting at the wrong crossing, and from the ferry landing the first roof he'll see is mine." She sets the lid on the box. "So I expect him by evening, and he will ask me what I've seen."

She turns round. There is something in her face that in a less dignified woman would be mischief.

"I won't lie to him. I took a vow, and besides I'm bad at it. But I can only tell a man what I know. If a traveller had asked me the road to Marrow Down, which is inland and two days from anywhere, then I could say with a clear conscience that a traveller asked me the road to Marrow Down." She folds her hands into her sleeves and raises one eyebrow, and waits.
I smile. "Sister, which is the road to Marrow Down?" Then I shoulder my pack. "And which way is Thornby?"

"Marrow Down," says Sister Avel gravely, pointing west with her whole arm, "is by the white stone and then straight on for two days. A dull town. They make rope." She holds the pose a moment longer, as if for a witness. Then, turning only her wrist, she points behind the hives.

"Thornby is the track through the birches, down off the heath. You'll sleep in the old drovers' shelter by the stream and be at the market by mid-morning. A crowd is a good place to be lost in and a poor place to be looked for, so keep that case out of sight if you can."

She presses something small into your hand: a clay pot no bigger than a walnut, sealed with wax. "Honey and yarrow. Fresh every evening, and let the air at it for an hour first." She has already pulled the veil down over her face and picked up her smoker. "Go well."

From the edge of the birches you can see back across the whole heath. On the road from the river, still half a mile from the shrine, a single figure is walking. It is too far to make out a face. There is a spot of red at its neck.
I reach Thornby by mid-morning and go into the market crowd, looking first for something to eat.

Thornby is one long sloping square with a stone well at the top and a town gate at the bottom, and on market day every yard between them is filled. There are geese in wicker crates, bolts of undyed wool, a man selling knives off a blanket, a dentist with a drum. The noise closes over you like water. Nobody looks twice at one more traveller with a pack.

The smell of hot fat leads you to a stall under a patched blue awning, where a round, red-armed woman is lifting pies out of a clay oven with a wooden peel.

"Mutton or eel, love, a penny each, penny ha'penny for the pair, and I'd not have the eel myself, it's Thursday's." She does not stop moving or talking. "You've walked far, I can tell by the boots. If it's boots you want, Jem's by the gate. If it's anything with a wheel or a spring in it, old Corwin Hale by the well, he mends clocks, there's nothing he can't open." She drops her voice no more than a little. "There's a gentleman in a grey coat been buying drinks at the Lamb since yesterday and asking after brass instruments, would you believe. Mutton, then?"
I buy a mutton pie and eat it on the way up to the well. At the instrument-maker's stall I put the compass on his counter. "Can you replace the glass on this?"

The stall by the well is a narrow booth hung with clock faces, each telling a different time. The man behind the counter is small and bald, with a jeweller's lens strapped to his forehead on a leather band. He says nothing at all until he has pulled the lens down, picked up the compass, and looked at it for a long while from every side.

"Fennick of Greywater made this. Forty years ago, maybe fifty. You can tell by the hinge." His voice is dry and precise. "The needle's sound and the pivot's clean. The glass I can cut in an hour, for sixpence. You were right to bring it; that crack has been letting the damp in, and one more winter would have spotted the card past reading."

He opens the lid and tilts it to the light. His eye rests on what is engraved inside, and then, briefly, on you. He does not read it aloud.

"A gift," is all he says. "People don't engrave what they buy for themselves." He sets the compass down on a square of green baize. "Corwin Hale. Will you wait, or come back for it? I'd say wait. It's not a thing I'd leave on a counter today."
"I'll wait." I count out the sixpence and stand where I can watch both his hands and the square.

Corwin works without hurry. He lifts the brass ring, tips the cracked glass out into his palm and sets it aside, then scores a new disc from a sheet with a diamond point, turning it against his thumb. The scratching is a small clean sound under the roar of the market.

He is polishing the edge when a man stops at the booth. He wears a grey coat of good cloth and carries his hat in his hand, and his manner is that of someone used to being welcome. He looks at the compass on the baize. He looks at the brass case on your back, for rather longer.

"A handsome case," he says pleasantly, to you and not to Corwin. "Forgive me. I act for a gentleman who collects survey work of this coast, and who pays for it better than any guild. He would give twenty pounds for whatever is in that tube, without unrolling it. Fifty, if the estuary is among it."

Corwin goes on polishing. He has not looked up, but the cloth is moving more slowly than before.

The man in the grey coat waits with his head a little on one side, smiling, as if the three of you had all the time in the world.
"It's not for sale. Tell your gentleman the Guild will publish the chart when it's finished, and he can buy a copy like everyone else." I hold out my hand to Corwin for the compass.

The smile does not change. If anything it grows a little kinder, which is worse.

"I'll tell him. Mr Dunmore is a patient man. I would not rely on his being a patient man next week." He puts his hat on, touches the brim to you, and adds, "Good day, surveyor." Then he walks down the square, unhurried, and stops at the steps of the market cross to speak to a stout fellow in a blue coat who holds a handbell.

Corwin sets the ring back on its seat with a click and lays the compass in your palm. The new glass is so clear it seems not to be there. Beneath it the needle swings, hesitates, and settles on north.

"The sixpence was for the glass." He pushes the lens back up onto his forehead and at last looks at you directly. "This costs nothing. There are two ways out of Thornby to the north. One is the gate, where everybody goes and anybody may stand and watch. The other is Tanners' Lane, behind the cross. It stinks so badly that no one who has a choice ever looks down it." He begins winding a clock, as though he had said nothing.
I tuck the compass inside my coat and stay near the well just long enough to hear what the crier is going to say.

The stout man in the blue coat climbs the steps of the market cross and swings his bell until the square is something close to quiet.

"Hear this! By the wish of Mr Dunmore of Greywater, shipowner! A reward of ten pounds in silver, for word of a surveyor, a woman, travelling north on the harbor road with a brass chart case! Wanted in the matter of instruments unlawfully removed! Ten pounds, to be paid at the Lamb!" He rings again and repeats it, word for word. There is no name in it either time. He has plainly not been given one.

A murmur goes through the crowd. Ten pounds is a year's wages for most of the people in this square. Heads begin to turn, idly at first, the way people look about them when they have been told there is a wasp.

Down the slope, the pie woman under the blue awning is staring straight at you across forty yards of market. Then, very deliberately, she looks down at her pies and begins rearranging them. At the bottom of the square two young men have moved to stand one on each side of the town gate, and are studying every face that passes through.
I pull up my hood, carry the map case low against my leg like a walking staff, and make for Tanners' Lane without hurrying.

Nobody stops you. The crowd is looking for a woman with a case on her back, and what passes the cross is a hooded traveller leaning on a stick.

Tanners' Lane announces itself ten yards before you reach it. The smell is a physical thing, sour and animal, thick enough to taste. The lane is a slot between two blind walls, running with brown water, and it opens into a yard of sunken vats where hides hang over poles like wet sails. A yellow dog on a chain gets up, thinks better of it, and lies down again.

A man is standing waist-deep in one of the vats, treading. He is stained the colour of oak bark to the shoulders. He looks at your hood, and then at the brass end of the thing in your hand, for exactly as long as it takes to understand it.

"Didn't see you," he says, and goes on treading. "Can't see a thing for the steam." He lifts one dripping arm toward a gap in the back wall, where a path climbs steeply through nettles toward open sky.

Behind you, muffled by the walls, the handbell starts up again.
I climb to the cliff path and keep going north as fast as I safely can, looking back at every bend.

The nettles give way to turf cropped short by sheep, and the wind arrives all at once, clean and cold after the tannery. The cliff path is a pale thread along the very edge of the land. On your left the ground simply ends. Two hundred feet below, the sea works at the rocks with a slow booming that you feel in your feet, and gulls turn in the air beneath you.

At the first bend there is nobody behind. At the second, nobody. At the third you can see all the way back to the town wall, and two small figures are coming out of the gap where the lane ends. It is too far to tell what they are wearing. They are not hurrying. They do not need to; there is only one path.

Then the light changes. Out over the water a bank of fog is coming in, flat-topped and solid as a harbour wall, and it reaches the cliff while you watch. The sea vanishes, then the gulls, then the path behind you. Within a few minutes you can see ten paces of wet turf and nothing more.

Just ahead the path divides. One branch keeps to the edge. The other climbs away to the right. Somewhere up that slope, a sheep's bell clanks.
I take out the compass, see which branch runs north, and follow it slowly, testing the ground ahead with the end of the map case.

Under the new glass the needle steadies at once. The branch along the edge runs a little east of north. The one that climbs bends away almost due east, inland, toward the bell.

The edge path it is. For fifty paces the turf is firm, and the end of the case knocks reassuringly on solid ground. The booming of the sea comes from everywhere at once now, and the fog has a taste of salt.

Then the case meets nothing. The turf in front of you is cracked like the crust of a loaf, and beyond the crack it tilts away into white. A stone the size of a fist, dislodged by the brass, rolls over the lip. You do not hear it land for a long time.

"Stop there!" The voice comes from above you in the fog, young and sharp and badly frightened. "Not one more step, that's the slip! It went in the spring and took six of ours with it!" There is a scramble of feet on wet grass, and the sheep's bell is suddenly much nearer. "Stand still. Just stand still, and I'll come down to you."
I stand perfectly still. "I'm not moving. Who's there?"

A shape comes down out of the white, sideways, the way hill people descend a slope: a girl of fourteen or so in an oilskin made for someone much larger, with a shepherd's crook in her fist. She stops well short of the cracked turf, reaches out with the crook, and hooks it firmly through the strap of your pack.

"Now come back toward me. Three steps. Don't look down, there's nothing to see." She does not let go until you are standing on the climbing path beside her, and then she lets out her breath in a rush.

"Wenna Garrow. That's my father's grazing you were about to walk off." Up close she has a wind-burned face and very pale eyebrows, and she is trying hard to look as though her hands are not shaking. A wet black-faced sheep with a bell at its neck has followed her down and stands watching you both without interest.

Wenna looks you over in turn. Her eyes stop on the long brass case. "Are you a pedlar? You've a pedlar's tube, for ribbons. Only pedlars know better than to take the edge path in a sea fret." She waits, crook planted, for you to account for yourself.
"A mapmaker. And thank you. I would have gone over." I look around at the fog. "Is there shelter anywhere near? I can't walk the cliff in this."

"A mapmaker." Wenna turns the word over, and evidently decides that it explains the foolishness without excusing it. "There's our fold, up the hill. Stone walls and a lean-to with a hearth. You're welcome to it. Nobody's turned out in a fret, that's the rule up here."

She does not move off, though. She is looking past you into the fog, chewing her lip.

"Only I can't go in yet. I'm one short. Bramble, she's my best ewe, and she's carrying out of season, and she went off on her own this afternoon the way they do when it's their time. If she lambs out in this, on her own, I'll lose the pair." She scrubs her nose with the back of her wrist. "I know every stone of this hill. In fog that's no use, I walk in rings the same as anybody."

Her eyes go to your coat, where the compass is. She must have seen the brass when you held it.

"You've a needle. You could keep a straight line. If you'd walk the slope with me, side to side, till we find her, you can have half my supper as well as the roof."
"Agreed. You call her, and I'll keep us on a line." I hold the compass flat in my palm and lead us across the slope in straight passes, east to west and back.

It is slow, cold work. The needle holds the line, and you count the paces of each pass while Wenna walks at your elbow with her head up, calling. It is a call with no words in it, three falling notes, and the fog swallows it a few yards out.

The first pass finds a boulder and a dead gorse bush. The second finds the black-faced bellwether again, which has followed and seems to think this a game. Wenna's calls grow shorter. She has stopped talking between them.

On the third pass something answers. It is a low, strained bleat, quite unlike the bellwether's, and it comes from below and to the left. Wenna is running before the sound has finished.

The ewe is lying on her side in a hollow under a bank of gorse, her flank heaving. Wenna drops to her knees in the wet, pushes back her sleeves, and looks. When she speaks her voice has gone flat and practical.

"It's coming backwards. I can turn it, I've done it twice. I need both hands for that, and I need someone at her head to hold her down, hard. She'll fight." She looks up at you through her wet hair.
I kneel at the ewe's head, lean my weight on her shoulder and talk to her quietly, keeping my bandaged arm clear of her legs.

Bramble's shoulder is hot and solid under your weight, and the wool is so wet it squeaks. She strains against you twice, hard, her hooves scoring the turf, and then lies trembling with one yellow eye rolled up at your face. Wenna works with her own eyes shut and her tongue between her teeth, saying "there, there, there" over and over to nobody in particular.

It takes a long time and then it takes no time at all. The lamb slides out onto the grass, slick and dark, and does not move. Wenna clears its mouth with one finger, picks it up by the hind legs and swings it, and rubs its ribs with a fistful of dry bracken from under the bank. It sneezes. Bramble heaves herself to her feet, shoving you aside, and begins to lick it.

Wenna sits back in the mud and grins, for the first time, from ear to ear.

Later, in the lean-to, with a fire of gorse roots and the oatcake broken in two, she tells you what lies ahead. "Two miles on there's the light, at the Point. The keeper's old Tane. Sour as sloes, but he'll not shut the door on you." She pokes the fire. "There were two men on the lower path at dusk, with a lantern, shouting to each other. They turned back. Were they after you?"
At first light I thank Wenna, leave her the last of my cheese, and walk the two miles to the lighthouse. I knock at the door at the foot of the tower.

The fog has thinned to a bright haze by the time the tower comes out of it: a white column streaked with rust, standing on a tongue of black rock with the sea on three sides. A low oil store and a wall of stacked driftwood huddle at its foot. High above, behind the glass, a light is still turning, pale in the daylight, and every minute a horn sounds one long flat note out to sea.

Your knock goes unanswered for some time. Then bolts are drawn, two of them, and the door opens a foot.

The keeper is very tall and badly stooped, a man of seventy with a white beard cut square and lamp-black worked deep into the creases of his hands. He looks at you as he might at a gull that had landed on his step.

"The light's lit and the horn's sounding. If you've come to complain of either, the Guild office is in Greywater, behind the fish market." His eyes move to the brass case on your back and rest there. Something in his face shifts, though it is not yet a welcome. "Ah. Or else you've come from the Guild. Which is it?"
"Hired by the Guild, yes, to chart the estuary. I was told the keeper here knows the bar better than anyone alive."

The door opens the rest of the way.

"Brannoch Tane. Thirty-one years on this light. You'd better come up." He does not wait to see whether you follow. The stair winds up inside the wall, worn hollow in the middle of each step, and he climbs it without touching the rail.

The watch room is round, whitewashed, and scrupulously neat: a stove, a cot, a table under the seaward window, a brass telescope on a bracket. Tane takes a ledger down from a shelf. It is bound in sailcloth and as thick as a family bible.

"Every vessel lost on the bar since the day I came. Nineteen. For each one, the bearing from this gallery to where she struck, the state of the tide, and the wind." He lays it on the table in front of you. "The Wren was the last. Eleven men. I have sent these figures to Greywater four times, and four times I was told that nobody could make a chart of them."

He keeps his hand flat on the cover.

"Before I lift this. When your chart is finished, who has it? The Guild, to print for any master with a shilling? Or some gentleman, to keep in a drawer and sell the knowledge by the tide?"
"The Guild, to publish. A man named Dunmore has offered me fifty pounds to do otherwise, and I've been walking away from his people for four days."

Tane looks at you for a long moment from under his eyebrows. Then he takes his hand off the ledger.

"Dunmore owns three pilot cutters, and he would like to own the bar as well. A man who alone knows the channel can charge what he pleases to bring a ship through it." He says it without heat, as a thing he has had many years to get used to. "Fifty pounds. He offered me a pension. Then the ledger is yours to copy, surveyor, every line."

He clears the table with two sweeps of his arm, lights a second lamp although it is day, and sets out a steel rule and a pair of brass dividers that look older than he is.

"The bearings are no use to you as figures. You'll want them plotted. I can read them out, it's my hand and nobody else can follow it." He nods at the window, where the haze is still hiding everything beyond the rocks. "And this will be gone by dark. Tomorrow, low water is at six. From the gallery, at first light, you will see the whole bar laid bare from end to end. It shows itself perhaps ten mornings in a year."

He folds his arms. "So. Copy first, or sleep first? You look as though you need both."
"Copy first." I spread a clean sheet on his table, mark the tower at its centre, and plot each wreck as he reads the bearings out, working late into the night.

He reads in a flat, careful voice, like a man reading a lesson in church: the name of the vessel, the year, the bearing, the tide. The Marigold. The Two Sisters. The Providence of Thornby, with a cargo of salt. Each one becomes a small pencilled cross under your hand, and Tane waits for the scratch of the pencil to stop before he goes on to the next.

By the twelfth cross there is a shape on the paper. By the nineteenth, which is the Wren, it cannot be mistaken: a long curve lying across the mouth of the estuary, hooked at its northern end, with one stretch near the hook where no cross falls at all.

Tane has come round the table to stand behind you. He is quiet for some time.

"There she is," he says at last. "Thirty-one years, and that's the first I ever saw her whole."

Near midnight he climbs to trim the lamp. You hear his boots on the iron gallery, and then they stop. His voice comes down the stairwell, pitched low.

"Lanterns on the cliff path. Two, coming from the Thornby side, and slowly. They'll be at my door within the hour." A pause. "The door is oak, and no one enters a light without the keeper's leave. But it's you they want. I'd hear what you wish done."
"Don't open to them. If they ask, a Guild surveyor is working here under the keeper's protection, and that's all. I'll take my bearings at dawn and be gone before they've decided what to do."

"That was my own thought," says Tane, and comes down.

The knocking begins a little before one. It is not loud; it is the knocking of men who would prefer to be thought reasonable. Tane takes a lamp and descends without haste. You hear the small iron grille in the door scrape open.

"Keeper." A thin voice, hoarse from the fog. "We're looking for a woman. A surveyor. There's ten pounds—"

"You're looking at a lighthouse." Tane's voice carries up the stair as flat as it was when he read the wrecks. "It is Guild property, and there is a surveyor here on Guild business. If you want her name you may apply to the Guild for it, since I have not asked it and do not mean to. Lay a hand on this door and I enter it in the log. The log goes to the harbour court every quarter day." The grille scrapes shut.

There is muttering outside, and then the sound of boots moving off. From the window you can see a lantern settle in the lee of the oil store and stay there.

Tane comes back up, sets a kettle on the stove, and puts two tin cups on the table beside the chart. "Four hours to low water," he says.
At first light I go out onto the gallery with my instruments and take bearings on both ends of the bar and on every break in the surf between them.

The fog is gone as if it had never been. The air is cold and so clear that the far shore of the estuary looks close enough to hit with a stone.

And the bar is there. With the tide at its lowest it lies across the river mouth exactly as the crosses said it would: a long hook of pale sand and broken white water, more than a mile from end to end. Two-thirds of the way along there is a place, no wider than a ship is long, where the water runs dark and smooth between the breakers.

Tane stands at your shoulder and names the marks as you sight on them. The square tower of the church in Greywater. The iron beacon on Gull Rock. The tall chimney of the old saltworks on the southern shore. Each bearing you take falls within a pencil's width of his nineteen crosses.

"The gap," he says, when you reach it. "There. With the church tower in line with the beacon, a vessel is in deep water all the way." He does not say anything about the Wren. He does not need to.

Far below, by the oil store, two men have got stiffly to their feet. They are looking up at the gallery, shading their eyes against the sunrise.
I ink in the channel, put my initials and the date in the corner of the sheet, and slide it into the map case. "Is there another way down from here, Brannoch?"

Tane watches you sign: two letters and a date. He reads them upside down and asks nothing about them. Something that might be approval crosses his face at being called by his first name, and is put away again.

"There is the keeper's stair." He takes you down past the watch room to the cellar, where barrels of lamp oil stand in rows, and hauls up a trapdoor by an iron ring. Cold air comes out of it, and the sound of water. "Cut in the rock by the men who built the tower. It comes out at the landing cove, where the supply boat ties up. They can't see the cove from the door."

He holds the lamp over the opening. "At low water there's a shingle beach under the cliff, all the way north to the sea chapel on the edge of Greywater. An hour's walk. When the tide turns, there's no beach, so you have until eight and not a minute past. The verger at the chapel is called Pask. He rings the Guild's bell and he'll take you to the hall."

From inside his coat he draws a folded paper, sealed with a blob of candle wax. "For the Guild master. It says the bearings are mine, and that the chart is honest." He holds it out to you over the dark square of the trapdoor.
I take the letter, shake his hand, and go down the keeper's stair to the beach, then walk north under the cliff as quickly as the shingle allows.

His hand is dry and hard as a plank. He says only, "Mind the ninth step, it's loose," and lowers the trapdoor after you.

The stair is wet, steep, and black as a well, with a tarred rope for a rail. It lets you out into a cove no bigger than a barn, where an iron ring is set in the rock and green water sucks at a stone ledge. Beyond it the shingle begins, a grey ribbon between the cliff and the sea, and it is hard going: the pebbles roll under your boots and every step slides half a pace back. When you look round, the tower is already small behind you. Two smaller figures are still standing at its door, waiting for it to open.

The chapel comes into view round the last headland: a squat building with a stone cross, perched on a shelf of rock, with a flight of steps climbing from it into a crowd of slate roofs and masts. One green copper dome rises above the rest. Behind you the first waves of the returning tide are reaching the foot of the cliff.

An old man in a rusty black coat is sweeping sand off the chapel steps. He leans on his broom to watch you come.

"You cut that fine, traveller. Nobody walks in by the beach but smugglers and keepers. Which are you?"
"Neither. A surveyor, with a letter for the Guild master from the keeper at the Point." I show him the wax seal without letting go of it. "He said you would take me to the hall."

The old man looks at the blob of candle wax for some time, and then at the wet shingle behind you, where the sea has already covered your last hundred footprints.

"That's Brannoch's seal. He's too mean to buy proper wax." He props the broom against the chapel door. "Pask. Verger here forty years, and bell-ringer to the Guild for thirty of them, which is the better-paid half. He's never sent me anybody by the beach before. I'd say that means you matter or you're in trouble."

He does not wait to be told which. He climbs the steps ahead of you at a surprising pace, talking over his shoulder. Greywater opens out above the chapel: steep lanes of slate and whitewash running down to a harbour crowded with masts, nets hung between the houses like washing, and everywhere the smell of tar and frying fish. People nod to Pask. Their eyes slide to the brass case on your back and stay on it a moment too long.

"They cried a reward in Thornby, we heard. Ten pounds. News comes up the coast faster than fish." He stops at a corner where the lane divides. To the left it drops to the quays. To the right it climbs to a square stone building with a green copper dome and a bell hanging in an arch above the door. "The front door is on the quay and half the town can see who goes in. There's a side door by the bell rope, and I have the key. Which will you have?"
"The side door. I've had enough of being looked at." I follow him up to it.

"Sensible," says Pask, and takes you round by an alley so narrow that the case scrapes both walls. The side door is low and iron-bound. He opens it with a key as long as his hand and lets you into a stone passage that smells of ink, damp wool and old paper.

The Guild hall is quieter inside than a church. Through an archway you can see one long room lined with pigeonholes, each stuffed with rolled charts, and a high desk where a young woman is copying figures into a ledger with her tongue between her teeth. She looks up at the sound of the door, sees Pask, and then sees what you are carrying. Her pen stops.

"Nell Harrow," Pask says to you, by way of introduction. "Clerk to the Guild. She knows where everything is, which is more than the master does." To her he says, "From the Point, by the beach, with a letter under Brannoch's seal. I'll be at my rope if I'm wanted," and he goes off down the passage without another word.

Nell climbs down from her stool. She is perhaps twenty-five, ink to the knuckles, with a quick, measuring look.

"You're the surveyor the agent engaged in the south. We had word a month ago that someone had been found, and then nothing at all. No name, even. The agent wrote that you'd asked for it to be kept out of the letters." She glances at the door behind you. "The master's upstairs with the pilots, and it's going badly. Do you want me to fetch him out, or will you wait until they've finished shouting?"
"Fetch him out. What I've brought will end the shouting, or start a better one." I unsling the map case and keep it in my hands.

Nell considers you for the length of a breath, then gathers her skirts and runs up the stairs two at a time. A door opens above. The noise of several men talking at once spills down the stairwell, and stops.

The man who comes down is past sixty, heavy in the shoulders, with a seaman's rolling walk and a landsman's good coat that he wears as though it belonged to somebody else. He has a pilot's pale, creased eyes. He takes in your boots, white with salt to the ankle, and the bandage at your cuff, and the case.

"Osric Dallow. Master of this Guild for my sins." His voice is deep and unhurried. "I've four senior pilots upstairs telling me the estuary can't be charted, because their fathers couldn't do it, and two telling me it mustn't be, because Dunmore has promised them shares. And now Nell says a surveyor has walked in off the beach with a letter from the one man on this coast who never writes to anybody."

He holds out a broad hand, palm up. It is not quite a demand.

"I'll read Tane's letter first, if you'll trust me with it. Then I'd like to know what's in that tube. And then," he adds, with the ghost of a smile, "you can tell me what I'm to call you, since my own agent wouldn't."

I give him the letter. While he reads, I unroll the dawn sheet on Nell's desk and weigh the corners with her inkwells. "Call me the surveyor. That's what I'm here to be. This is the bar at low water, taken from the gallery two mornings ago, with nineteen wrecks plotted from the keeper's ledger."

Dallow breaks the wax with his thumb and reads standing, his lips moving slightly. It is a short letter. He reads it twice, folds it into his breast pocket, and comes to the desk.

Nobody speaks for a while. Nell has put the back of her wrist against her mouth. Dallow leans on his knuckles over the sheet and follows the long hooked line of the bar from one end to the other without touching it, the way a man looks at the face of someone he has only ever heard described.

"Nineteen," he says at last. "I knew men on eleven of those." His finger hovers above the place, two-thirds along, where no cross falls. "And this. Tane's letter says a gap, with the church tower in line with the beacon. My grandfather used to swear there was a way through on the ebb. They laughed at him until he stopped saying it."

He straightens up. The slow voice has not changed, but something behind it has.

"Surveyor it is. Now hear the hard part. This is a sketch from a tower, and a fine one. No master will take a loaded ship through a gap on the strength of a sketch. I need depths. Soundings across that channel at low water and at high, on a spring tide, laid down so that any fool with a lead line can check them. The next springs are in six days." He looks at you steadily. "Can it be done in six days? Tell me the truth; I've had enough of the other thing this morning."

"It can, with a boat that draws little, a skipper who'll go where I ask, and two clear tides. I'll need a lead line I've measured myself and someone to call the marks. What I can't promise is the weather."

"Nobody on this coast promises the weather. That you didn't try is the first thing you've said that makes me believe the rest." Dallow turns to Nell. "The Kittiwake. Is Penhale in?"

"Came in on the morning flood. He'll be asleep or at the Anchor." Nell is already pulling a ledger toward her. "He won't like it."

"He doesn't like anything. It's why he's still alive." To you Dallow says, "Jory Penhale has the smallest cutter we own and the best hands. He's taken her closer to the bar than any man living, and he'll tell you at length that what you're asking is madness. Let him tell you. Then show him that sheet."

He rolls the chart himself, with great care, and holds it a moment before giving it back.

"One thing more. That reward they cried is Dunmore's, and Dunmore sits on the harbour bench with two other magistrates. He owns three cutters, the ropewalk, and the notes of half the men upstairs. He will not send a thin fellow in a scarf to follow you about, here. He'll do it with paper." Dallow nods toward an iron door set in the wall behind Nell's desk. "The Guild has a strongroom. That sheet would be safer in it than on your back. But it's your work and your choice, and I won't take it from your hands."
I think about it, then hold the rolled sheet out to Nell. "The strongroom. But I'd like a receipt, and I keep my field notes with me."

"You'll have one in my hand and under the Guild's seal," says Nell, with evident approval. She takes the roll as if it were made of glass.

The strongroom door needs two keys, hers and Dallow's, turned together. Inside there is a space no bigger than a pantry, shelved with deed boxes and smelling of cold iron. Nell lays the chart flat in a long drawer by itself, locks the drawer, and writes out the receipt at her desk in a fast clear script: one sheet, survey of the bar at low water, received from the Guild's surveyor this day, to be released to her alone. Dallow presses the seal into the wax himself, a ship's wheel with an eye at the hub.

"Released to her alone," he reads over, and nods. "Good. If any man comes here with a paper saying otherwise, he'll have to break the door, and then he'll have to explain the door."

From above comes the scrape of chairs. The pilots have grown tired of waiting. Dallow glances at the ceiling with the patience of a man looking at a leak.

"I must go back up and tell them that their grandfathers were wrong and mine was right. It'll take the rest of the day." He pauses with a hand on the stair rail. "Nell will find you a bed. There's the Anchor, where the whole harbour drinks and Penhale can be found. Or there's Widow Sabel's, over the chandlery, which is clean and quiet and has a bolt on the door. You'll know best which suits you."
"The widow's. I'll find Penhale at the Anchor once I've washed four days of road off." I turn to Nell. "Show me the way?"

Nell takes a shawl from a peg and leads you out by the side door, locking it behind her. She walks fast and talks faster, pointing with her chin.

"Ropewalk, that long shed. That's his. The three black cutters at the east quay with the yellow stripe, his. The tall house with the green shutters above the fish market is his too, and he'll have known you were in the town before you'd climbed the chapel steps." She says it without drama. "He isn't a monster. People will tell you he is. He pays his men on the day and he buried the Wren's crew out of his own pocket. He just can't abide a thing he doesn't own."

The chandlery stands on the corner of the middle quay, its window stacked with coiled line, lanterns and tins of tallow. A bell jangles as Nell pushes the door. Behind the counter a small, straight-backed woman of seventy is weighing nails into a paper twist. She finishes the weighing before she looks up.

"Guild lodger, Mother Sabel. A week at least. She's to have the back room with the bolt."

"Is she." Widow Sabel studies you over a pair of steel spectacles: the salt, the bandage, the brass case. "Ninepence a night with breakfast, and you'll take those boots off at the foot of my stairs. I ask two things of lodgers. No tallow candles in the room, they stink. And if anybody comes asking for you at my door, do I know you or don't I?"

I take off my boots at the foot of the stairs. "You don't know me. You've a lodger who pays on time and keeps to herself. And I need to buy sixty fathoms of your best sounding line and a seven-pound lead."

"Then I've never set eyes on you," says Widow Sabel placidly, "and you owe me ninepence."

She comes out from behind the counter to serve you herself. The line she takes down is pale new hemp, hard-laid, and she runs a length of it between her thumb and finger before she lets you touch it. "Wet it and stretch it before you mark it, or your fathoms will all be short by evening. My husband marked lines for the Guild thirty years. Leather at two and three, white rag at five, red at seven, leather with a hole at ten. I've the rags and the leather, if you want to do it properly."

The lead she sets on the counter with both hands. It is a long grey plummet with a hollow in its foot. "That's for the tallow. Arm it and it brings you up a pinch of the bottom, sand or shell or mud. A depth tells you how much water. The bottom tells you where you are."

Nell has gone, with a quick nod from the door. The widow wraps the lead in sacking, pushes line and rags across to you, and totals it on a slate.

"Back room's up two flights. The window looks on the yard, not the quay; I thought you'd prefer it." She takes off her spectacles and regards you without them, which is somehow sharper. "There's a measured fathom cut in the flagstones of my yard. His doing. You can stretch your line there this afternoon, or you can sleep. You look as though you ought to sleep. Which is it to be?"
"The line first. I won't trust depths taken with a line I haven't measured." I carry it out to the yard, soak it in the rain butt, and stretch it along the flagstones.

The yard is a walled square with a pump, a rain butt and a row of pots where somebody grows parsley. The measured fathom is there as promised: two brass studs let into the flagstones six feet apart, worn bright by thirty years of rope.

Wet hemp is heavy and unwilling. You haul each length taut between the studs and it creeps, as the widow said it would, a finger's width in every fathom. By the time the sun has moved off the wall you have gone the full sixty twice over, and the line lies in long loops across the yard, darker and harder than when it left the shop.

Widow Sabel comes out with a bowl of barley broth and stands watching while you eat it. She says nothing until you take up the first strip of leather. Then she kneels, stiffly, and shows you the hitch her husband used, tucked through the strands so that it cannot slide.

"Two tails of leather at two fathoms. Three at three. Then your rags." Her fingers are quicker than yours. "A leadsman doesn't look at his line at night. He feels what's in his hand. So every mark must tell a different story to the thumb."

She sits back. The shop bell has jangled, and she is listening to it.

"That's a man's step, and he hasn't called out. Customers call out." She gets to her feet, brushing her skirt. "Stay here and go on with your marks, or come and see who it is. I can't tell you which is wiser."
I stay where I am, out of sight of the shop door, and keep working, but I listen.

The widow goes in, leaving the yard door ajar by the width of a hand. Through it you can see a slice of the shop: a shelf of lanterns, the corner of the counter, and now and then her elbow.

The voice that answers her greeting is pleasant and unhurried, and you have heard it before, over an instrument-maker's stall with the market roaring behind it.

"Good afternoon, ma'am. A pound of your white candles, if you please. And perhaps you can help me in another way. I'm looking for a lady, lately arrived, who may be in want of lodgings. A surveyor. She carries a brass case."

"Candles are fourpence," says Widow Sabel. Paper rustles. "I let one room, to seamen's widows from the country, when I let it at all. I don't know any surveyors. I shouldn't think there are any. It's not work for a woman."

"Indeed not. It is hardly work for anyone, in my employer's view." Coins are set down, one at a time. "If she should come by, perhaps you'd tell her that Mr Fitch called, and that Mr Dunmore would be glad to give her dinner. Tomorrow, at seven. He bears no ill will. He asked me to say so particularly."

The bell jangles. The widow does not come back at once. When she does, she is carrying your boots, which had been standing at the foot of her stairs in plain view of the counter.

"He looked at these," she says. "He was too polite to mention them. Well. You've been asked to dinner. Shall you go?"
"Not tomorrow, and not before I have depths in my notebook. Let him wonder." I tie off the ten-fathom mark and coil the line. "First I need my skipper. How do I know Penhale when I see him?"

"You'll hear him first. He'll be the one telling a room why something can't be done." The widow hands you the boots. "Lean, grey, a face like a shut door. He lost two fingers off his right hand to a parted hawser and he'll hold his pot in the other. Don't flatter him, he can't bear it. And don't tell him I sent you, I refused him credit in the spring."

The Anchor is three doors along the quay, a long low room with a fire at each end and a ceiling black with smoke. At this hour it is half full: pilots in blue jerseys, a table of ropewalk men, two women mending a net across their knees while they drink. The talk drops a little when you come in with the coiled line over your shoulder, and then picks up again, pitched slightly differently.

He is at the settle nearest the far fire. The widow's description would do for a warrant. He is speaking to a broad young deckhand and a boy of about thirteen, tapping the table with the three fingers of his right hand at every other word.

"...because the ebb sets across it at four knots, that's why, and there's no holding ground, and any man who says there is has never tried to hold." He becomes aware of you, standing at the end of his table. His eyes go to the line, and to the marks on it, and he reads them the way other men read print.

"That's a sounding line. New, and wet-stretched, and marked by someone who was shown how." He does not ask you to sit. "Who's it for?"

"For the Kittiwake, if her skipper will have it aboard. I'm the Guild's surveyor. Dallow says you've been closer to the bar than any man living, and that you'll tell me what I want is madness. I'd like to hear it."

The deckhand laughs, and stops when Penhale looks at him.

"Dallow says." Penhale turns his pot a quarter turn on the table. "Sit down, then. You asked. I never refuse to tell anyone they're a fool."

He tells you. It takes some time and it is very precise. The bar shifts after every northerly gale, so that what is true in March is a lie by May. The ebb runs across it, as he said, at four knots on a spring tide, and the flood hardly slower. There is a place where the seas break in a line as straight as a ruler, and another, farther north, where they do not break, which every pilot's son is taught to leave alone because smooth water over a bar means only that the sand is waiting an inch beneath. He has seen the Wren's mainmast standing out of it at low water. He was the one who took the Kittiwake in to look for men, and found none.

The boy has heard all this before and is watching you instead, to see how you take it.

"So," Penhale finishes. "Sixty fathoms of new line, and a lead, and a notebook. And you'd like me to sail my cutter, which draws five feet, into the smooth place, and stop there, at low water, while you count." He leans back. "That's what you came to ask. Isn't it?"

"Yes. But look at this before you answer." I open my field notebook to the copy of the wreck plot and the dawn bearings and turn it toward him on the table. "Nineteen wrecks from Tane's ledger. Not one in the smooth place."

Penhale does not pick the notebook up. He pulls the candle closer with his good hand and bends over the page, and the table goes quiet around him. The deckhand cranes to see. The boy slides off the bench and comes round to look under his skipper's arm, and is not sent away.

It is a small copy, in pencil, but the shape is plain: the hook of the bar, the nineteen crosses strung along it like beads on a wire, and the one bare stretch near the northern end. Penhale puts a three-fingered hand flat beside it, not on it. He finds the Wren without being shown. He looks at that cross for a long time.

"Tane kept these," he says. "All these years. The sour old devil, he never said." His finger moves to the gap. "She struck here. Two cables south of your bare patch. If she'd been two cables north..." He does not finish it.

The boy says, in a clear voice, "That's where Granfer said. Where the water goes dark."

"Your granfer said a great many things, Tam." But Penhale has not taken his eyes from the page. When he does look up, the shut door of his face has opened by perhaps an inch.

"I'll not take her in on the ebb. Nobody will. Slack water, low, there's twenty minutes when the bar holds its breath, and we creep in on sweeps with the boat ahead sounding. If the lead says less than two fathoms we come out, and you don't argue." He taps the table once. "Those are my terms. I don't bargain them."
"I accept them, all of them. I call the marks into the notebook, you decide when we leave. When is the next low slack we can use?"

"Tomorrow, twenty past five in the morning. After that, half past five in the evening, and the light'll be going." Penhale drains his pot and stands. He is taller than he looked sitting down. "Morning, then. We warp off the Guild quay at four. If you're not aboard I'll assume you've come to your senses."

He names the others with a jerk of his head. The broad young man is Hob, two years in the Kittiwake, strong on a sweep and sound in a blow. The boy is Tam, his sister's son, who has the best ear for a lead line in the harbour and knows it.

"Tam calls the depth. That's his work and he's better at it than you'll be, so let him. You write." Penhale picks up the end of your line and runs it through his fingers as the widow did, mark by mark, with his eyes on the fire. At the ten-fathom leather he stops and gives a short grunt that might be approval. "Sabel's hitch. So that's where you're lodged. I'll not tell anyone; she'd refuse me candles as well as credit."

Hob has got up too, and is looking at the notebook, still open on the table, with frank interest.

"Is it true there's ten pounds on you, miss?" he asks. He seems to mean nothing by it. "Only they were saying at the ropewalk. Ten pounds'd buy a share in a boat."

Penhale turns his head slowly and looks at him. The boy Tam looks at you.
I close the notebook and put it inside my coat before I answer. "It's true. It'll be more by the end of the week. Is that going to be a difficulty, Hob?"

Hob goes red to the ears. He is not more than twenty, and it is plain that he has only now heard how his question sounded.

"No, miss. I never meant... I only wondered." He looks to his skipper for help and gets none. "I'm Guild. My father was Guild. I wouldn't."

"He wouldn't," Penhale agrees, flatly, "because he knows I'd hear of it, and because nobody who sold a Guild surveyor would ever get a berth on this coast again, not with Dunmore either. Dunmore doesn't trust a man who can be bought. He just buys him." He drops a coin on the table for the ale. "Go and see to the sweeps, Hob. And grease the thole pins, I'll want her quiet."

Hob goes, gratefully. Penhale watches the door close after him.

"He's a good hand and he talks too much. That's all it is." He turns up the collar of his coat. "But I'd keep that book where it is, in your coat, and I'd not show it across a table in the Anchor again. I was glad to see it. So were six other people."

He is right. Around the room, heads have turned back to their own business a little too smoothly. By the door a man is getting up to leave, in no hurry, drawing on a pair of gloves. His coat is grey.

Tam tugs at your sleeve. "Miss. I can show you a way back to Mother Sabel's that doesn't go along the quay. Through the net lofts. Nobody goes that way but cats." He glances at his uncle, who shrugs.
"Lead on, Tam. And tell me about your grandfather on the way. I want to hear what he said about the dark water."

Tam takes you out through the Anchor's scullery, past a startled woman plucking a gull, and up an outside stair into the lofts. They run the whole length of the quay above the shops: one long dim attic after another, joined by plank doors, hung from end to end with drying nets like brown curtains. It smells of tar and fish scales. Tam goes through it at a trot, ducking the floats without looking.

"Granfer was a pilot before the Guild had cutters. He used to take the boat out on a calm day and look. He said the water on the bar's all one colour, like milk with tea in it, except one place where it goes dark like a horse's eye. He said dark means deep." Tam holds a net aside for you. "He told the master before this one. They said it was weed. He said weed moves and this didn't. He drew it on the table in ale once and my mam wiped it off."

He stops at a hatch in the floor and lifts it. Below is the widow's yard, the pump, the brass studs catching the last of the light.

"He's dead now. He'd have liked your book." The boy hesitates, one hand on the hatch. Something has been working in him since the Anchor, and it comes out in a rush. "Uncle Jory won't say, but the Wren's master was his brother. That's why he went in for them. That's why he knows it can't be done." He looks up at you, anxious and fierce together. "It can, though. Can't it?"
"It can be measured, Tam. Whether it can be sailed is what the measuring will tell us. Be at the quay at four and call me every mark, even the ones your uncle won't like." I climb down into the yard.

Tam grins, pulls the hatch shut over your head, and is gone; you hear him running back through the lofts.

The night is short. Widow Sabel wakes you with a knuckle on the door at half past three, and has bread and a mug of hot milk on the counter when you come down with the line over your shoulder and the lead in its sacking. She has drawn the bolts already. Outside, the quay is black and wet, and the only light is the lantern at the Kittiwake's masthead.

She is smaller than you expected: thirty feet of tarred cutter with a mast too tall for her and a nine-foot boat towing astern. Penhale is at the tiller. Hob and Tam are standing by the lines. Nobody says good morning. Penhale looks at the sky, a paler black to the east, and at the weed streaming from the quay piles.

"Ebb's nearly done. Cast off." The cutter slides out from the wall under two long sweeps, quiet as he wanted, and the harbour mouth opens ahead, grey on grey.

Beyond the pier head the swell takes her. Far out to the left a white light turns steadily: the Point. Ahead and to the right there is a sound like a long sheet of cloth being torn, over and over. Penhale nods toward it.

"That's her. You'll see her in a quarter hour." He glances at the bundle in your arms. "Arm your lead now, while your hands are warm. And tell me where you want the first cast. It's your survey."

I press tallow into the foot of the lead. "Start well outside, in water you know, so I can prove the line against a depth you trust. Then straight in along the line of the church tower and the beacon."

"Prove the line," Penhale repeats. It is the first thing you have said that he seems to find wholly reasonable. "The Outer Road is nine fathoms at low springs, sand and shell. Every pilot here has had that in his hand since he was Tam's age. Hob, bring her to."

The sweeps check. Tam takes the lead from you with a look that asks permission and is not really waiting for it. He swings it twice and lets it fly forward of the bow, and the new line runs out through his fingers, hissing. When it goes slack he hauls it up and down once to feel the bottom, and reads the mark at the waterline with his thumb, in the dark.

"By the deep, nine!" His voice cracks on it and he scowls. He brings the lead aboard and holds its foot to the lantern: grey sand, and a speck of broken shell, bedded in the tallow.

"Nine and shell," says Penhale. "Your line tells the truth. Write it."

The light is coming. The tearing sound has a shape now: a long low line of white, perhaps half a mile off, running north and south as far as you can see, and rising and falling like something breathing. Behind it the water of the estuary lies flat and pale. The cutter creeps toward it under her sweeps. Tam casts again without being told.

"And a half, seven! ... By the mark, seven! ... Six!"

Penhale has not once looked at the white water. He is looking back over his shoulder, at the town, lining something up. "Tower's coming on the beacon," he says. "A minute more. Are you ready with that book?"
I brace myself against the mast with the notebook open and the pencil tied to my wrist. "Ready. Call the marks and I'll take the time and the bearing at each one."

For some minutes there is nothing in the world but Tam's voice, the knock of the sweeps, and the pencil. The square tower of the church slides behind the iron beacon on Gull Rock until the two stand one above the other like the sights of a gun, and Penhale holds them there with small movements of the tiller.

"By the mark, five! ... Five! ... And a quarter, four!"

The bar is close now. To the south the seas heap up and fall over in a long ruled line, just as he described it in the Anchor, and the spray drifts across the deck like cold smoke. Directly ahead, between two shoulders of broken water, there is a lane perhaps a ship's length wide where the swell lifts and passes and does not break. In the growing light it is a different colour from everything around it. Tam's grandfather had it right. It is as dark as a horse's eye.

"Four! ... Four! ... By the mark, three!"

Hob has stopped breathing through his nose. Penhale's face is the shut door again.

"Two fathoms and we come out," he says. "I told you." The cutter moves into the lane. The noise of the surf closes in on both sides and the water under the bow goes smooth and black.

Tam swings, and lets go. The line runs. It keeps running. He stares at his hands.

"Uncle Jory," he says, in quite a different voice. "She's still taking it."
"Let it run, Tam. Give me the mark when she touches, whatever it is." I keep my eyes on the line and my pencil on the page.

The rags go out through the boy's fingers one after another: white, red. Then the line stops, and lifts, and he plumbs it up and down twice to be certain, his whole body bent over the bow.

"By the mark, seven!" It comes out as a shout. "Seven fathom, Uncle Jory! Seven!"

Nobody answers him. Penhale's three-fingered hand has closed very hard on the tiller. Seven fathoms is forty-two feet of water, in a place where every chart in the Guild hall is blank and every pilot's son is taught there is an inch.

"Again," says Penhale. "Other side. Hob, a stroke to starboard, no more."

"And a half, six! ... By the deep, six! ... Seven again!"

Tam brings the lead in and holds it to the lantern, and the foot of it is clean. There is no sand in the tallow at all, only three or four black flakes like chips of slate, and a scratch across the lead itself, bright and new.

"Rock," says Hob.

"Scoured," says Penhale slowly. "The ebb's been coming through here so long it's swept the bottom bare. That's why there's no holding. I told them there was no holding. I never thought to ask why." He looks at the two walls of surf, one on each hand, and then at you, and for the first time there is nothing shut in his face at all.

"You have perhaps twelve minutes of slack left. After that the flood comes through this lane like a millrace and takes us with it. I can give you a line straight through to the inside, or back and forth across to find the edges. Not both. Choose."
"Across. A channel is only as good as its edges, and I can run the length of it tomorrow. Take us from wall to wall as many times as the slack allows."
